title: How to approach Tatum: master all twelve keys
summary: Wilson advises pianists to learn everything in all keys and recalls Tatum's transposition, touch and inspiring effect.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Uh huh. A lot of pianists ask me about that Tatum thing, and I say the best thing I know how to become like Tatum is just learn everything you know on all

12 keys, be able to become a master of transposition, because that's what he had -- he had that harmony thing under his fingers where he could -- you know, he used to play 'Tea for Two' and change the key every two bars.
And make it come right back home as evenly as a fine patchwork.
Just phenomenal. I still can't get over Tatum; I don't think there's been a phenomenon like him since.
Never, never. The taste and the dignity of that guy.

The touch, too. For a person who learned the harmonic system -- when you hear them play, the finesse of the touch is not there like Tatum had. Tatum's name was written on his touch and the other things all working together there.
Yeah. I remember a dear friend of yours and mine, Ben Webster -- who always used to say to me, 'I'd get up every morning, and to get my life started, I play a Tatum record.'

Sure. I found him to be a tremendous stimulus to me, because if I never heard Tatum I would never have dreamed that music could sound like that; I had no conception that music could be like that. But when I hear a Tatum record,

it opened a whole door to another world that had such possibilities. And he inspired me. A lot of players I met said they were going to be a piano player, but when they heard Art Tatum, they quit. I don't understand that -- because he made me want to play the piano.
